title: Exciton superfluidity in two-dimensional bilayers at zero and high magnetic fields
abstract: We study interlayer exciton superfluidity versus layer separation in two-dimensional electron-hole bilayers at zero magnetic field and quantum Hall bilayers at total filling $ν_T=1$. Unscreened Hartree-Fock theory predicts coherence at every finite separation, with an energy scale decaying inversely with separation at large distances. We examine how screening, correlations, and spatial instabilities modify this prediction. At zero field, we solve the linearized gap equation with the full momentum and frequency dependence of the interaction screened within the random-phase approximation, without an imposed cutoff. The apparent plasmon enhancement of pairing in the ladder approximation is largely cancelled by the second-order crossed-rung correction. Static screening determines the leading pairing exponent in the controlled high-density limit at fixed separation. At large separation, the pairing scale falls exponentially with squared separation while the instability persists. Extending this result to fixed density assumes Fermi-liquid layers and higher-order dynamical corrections subleading to the static pairing interaction. At high field, we obtain an analytic uniform Hartree-Fock saddle point in the lowest Landau level, coherent at every finite separation. Within Hartree-Fock theory, its finite-wave-vector collective-mode instability favors an excitonic supersolid, distinguishing loss of spatial uniformity from loss of coherence. We conjecture that the quantum Hall bilayer evolves continuously toward weak pairing of composite fermions, with a scale far below the mean-field prediction at large separation. This suppression could produce an apparent critical separation at finite temperature without a ground-state quantum phase transition. The comparison separates the existence, energy scale, and spatial stability of interlayer coherence.
summary: This paper theoretically examines exciton superfluidity in 2D electron-hole bilayers under varying magnetic fields and layer separations. Using advanced many-body techniques, it contrasts mean-field predictions with correlation effects, finding that while coherence is predicted broadly, the actual pairing scale shows strong separation dependence. The findings help delineate the stability and nature of interlayer quantum phases in these correlated systems.
main_problem: The study investigates the evolution of interlayer exciton superfluidity in two-dimensional electron-hole bilayers, comparing behavior at zero magnetic field to the quantum Hall regime.
main_result: The theory predicts that while mean-field theory suggests coherence persists across all separations, detailed analysis shows the pairing scale decays exponentially at large separations, and the high-field case favors an excitonic supersolid instability.
method: The authors employ advanced many-body techniques, including solving the linearized gap equation using the Random-Phase Approximation (RPA) and analyzing Hartree-Fock (HF) saddle points.
model_or_system: The system is a two-dimensional electron-hole bilayer, analyzed in two limits: zero magnetic field (semiconductor-like) and high magnetic field at total filling $\nu_T=1$ (quantum Hall bilayer).
key_observables: Interlayer coherence/superfluidity, pairing energy scale, and the nature of collective instabilities (e.g., supersolid formation).
important_parameters: Layer separation ($d$), magnetic length ($\ell$), and filling factor ($\nu_T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies heavily on Hartree-Fock theory and RPA, with comparisons made to more rigorous treatments that account for screening and correlations.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the theoretical predictions for interlayer coherence across different regimes: zero field, high field ($\nu_T=1$), and discusses the implications of screening and correlation corrections in each limit.
why_interesting: The work tackles the complex interplay between mean-field predictions and correlation effects in strongly interacting 2D electron systems, which is central to understanding exotic quantum phases in condensed matter.
